reason: Both convert a natural-language shopping request into structured product constraints for downstream search.
The parser extracts structured constraints that the search formulator turns into practical search keywords.
The interpreter identifies requirements that the search constructor uses to build a concrete search action string.
Both synthesize search text from structured criteria, differing mainly in output format and prompt style.
Executing a search requires a usable keyword query from the formulator.
Search execution ultimately issues a formatted interface action through the generic action executor.
Product search relies on the lower-level executor to submit the search action and fetch results.
Initial search is a narrower first-pass version of the broader product-search skill.
Initial search needs a compact, platform-ready search string before submitting the first query.
After retrieving search results, the analyzer helps interpret which listings are worth pursuing.
Both review result listings against user constraints to identify promising candidate products.
Both narrow a search results page to items that best satisfy the target attributes and constraints.
Selecting the best product candidate assumes a prior shortlist or ranking from result analysis.
Filtering reduces the candidate pool that the product selector then chooses from.
Pagination is typically triggered after filtering shows that the current results page lacks a viable match.
Moving between result pages requires issuing a concrete click action through the action executor.
After a product is selected from results, the next step is to navigate into its detail page.
Opening a product detail page requires executing a specific click action.
Detail navigation is usually followed by a broader validation pass over the loaded product page.
Once the detail page is open, the inspector can verify fine-grained fields and selectable options.
Both inspect a product detail page for requirement match, with the inspector being slightly more interaction-oriented.
Attribute verification is a focused subset of the broader product detail checking workflow.
A detail check often includes an explicit budget validation step using the price checker.
Inspection of the detail page naturally feeds into selecting the correct option or variant.
After choosing an option, attribute verification confirms the page now reflects the desired configuration.
Attribute selection is a more specific case of the broader option-selection capability.
Variant choosing is a narrower specialization of option selection on product detail pages.
Both skills specialize in selecting detail-page variants such as size, color, quantity, or flavor.
Selecting an option requires issuing a click action through the generic action executor.
Attribute selection is realized as a concrete click action on the page.
Variant choice must be applied through a concrete page interaction.
Both culminate in triggering the final buy action once the product is confirmed.
Once the detail page has been validated, the purchase initiator carries the workflow into checkout.
Purchase initiation is usually preceded by a final verification that the selected attributes match the request.
The initiator often depends on a last budget confirmation before clicking the buy button.
Completing the purchase requires a final click action through the generic action executor.
Initiating checkout ultimately uses the same click-action primitive as other UI interaction skills.
